The Cape short-eared gerbil (Desmodillus auricularis) is a nocturnal rodent inhabiting the arid regions of southern Africa, where it occupies burrow systems that buffer against extreme surface temperatures. Field studies conducted in the Kalahari Desert have documented the species' reproductive biology under controlled laboratory conditions that simulate the stable microclimate of its subterranean environment. At a constant ambient temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], gestation in this species lasts 29 days [tg = 29 days], a relatively short period compared to other murid rodents of similar body mass. The neonatal pups emerge from the uterus weighing a mere 2.2 grams [Wwb = 2.2 grams], placing them among the smallest altricial newborns within the Gerbillinae subfamily. This low birth mass is consistent with the pattern observed in desert-adapted rodents, where rapid postnatal growth is favoured over extended intrauterine development given the ephemeral availability of resources in the environment. Lactation commences immediately following parturition, and the mother invests substantial metabolic effort into milk production during the earliest phase of offspring development.

The postnatal development of Desmodillus auricularis proceeds through a series of well-defined milestones, each linked to the energetic constraints imposed by the desert habitat. Under the same thermal regime of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the age at which the pups achieve nutritional independence from milk occurs at 33 days since birth [tx = 33 days since birth]. This weaning period is somewhat protracted relative to other small-bodied gerbils, perhaps reflecting the need for the nursing female to allocate resources judiciously in an environment where food patches are sparse and unpredictable. The weaned juveniles then undergo a phase of rapid somatic growth, during which they accumulate body mass while learning to forage on seeds and insects. Observations from captive colonies indicate that the transition from a milk-based diet to solid food is a gradual process, with the young initially supplementing their diet with small quantities of grain before fully weaning. This dietary shift marks the beginning of the juvenile stage.

Sexual maturation in the Cape short-eared gerbil occurs after a sustained period of post-weaning growth, with the onset of puberty observed at 77 days since birth [tp = 77 days since birth] under laboratory conditions held at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This age at puberty is somewhat later than that recorded for some other desert-dwelling rodents, potentially correlating with the species' moderate body size and life-history strategy emphasising survivorship over rapid turnover. The attainment of reproductive maturity coincides with the completion of most skeletal growth, after which the animals reach their ultimate wet weight of 54.5 grams [Wwi = 54.5 grams]. This adult mass is typical for a gerbil of its lineage and reflects a body plan adapted for efficient thermoregulation and locomotion across sandy substrates. Body mass in reproductively active adults remains relatively stable throughout the breeding season, although females may exhibit modest fluctuations related to pregnancy and lactation demands.

Reproductive output in Desmodillus auricularis is characterised by relatively small litters and a moderately paced breeding frequency, a pattern that aligns with the species' desert adaptation. Females typically produce 3.3 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3.3 pups per litter], a figure that is comparatively low among gerbils but consistent with the energetic constraints of rearing young in an oligotrophic environment. Litter size shows little variation across studies, suggesting a canalised reproductive strategy. The frequency of reproductive events is estimated at 4 litters per year [F_R_i = 4 litters per year], yielding a modest annual recruitment that is offset by relatively high adult survival. This combination of moderate litter size and repeated breeding attempts within a single year allows the population to persist during years of favourable rainfall while avoiding the high metabolic costs associated with larger clutches. The reproductive season typically coincides with the summer rains, when food availability peaks.

Longevity records for the Cape short-eared gerbil indicate that individuals can reach a maximum lifespan of approximately 6.1 years [am = approximately 6.1 years] when maintained under stable thermal conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This lifespan is notably extended for a rodent of its body size, exceeding the expectations derived from general allometric scaling relationships for small mammals. The relatively long life expectancy is likely an adaptation to the unpredictable desert environment, where favourable breeding conditions may arise sporadically, and iteroparous reproduction across multiple seasons maximises lifetime fitness. Senescence in captive individuals is gradual, with a decline in fecundity observed after the fourth year of life. Physiological studies suggest that the species exhibits a low basal metabolic rate compared to mesic-dwelling congeners, a trait that may contribute to its extended longevity by reducing cumulative oxidative damage over the organism's lifetime. Comparative data from related species underscore the uniqueness of this gerbil's life-history syndrome.
